title: Cost and Revenue
summary: Cost is the money a producer spends to buy or hire factors of production and raw materials to produce goods and services. It is the producer's sacrifice.
Example: a farmer pays ₹5,000 rent for land, ₹31,500 in wages, ₹3,000 for seeds and fertiliser and ₹2,500 for a tractor. The total cost is ₹42,000 for 30 quintals of rice.
Fixed cost is spending on fixed factors, such as rent for land or a tractor. It is compulsory and has nothing to do with the amount of output; it must be paid even if nothing is produced.
Variable cost is spending on variable factors, such as wages and raw materials. It changes with output.

Explicit cost is the money actually paid out for fixed and variable factors and raw materials. These are direct payments, properly calculated and recorded with bills and receipts. Rent paid is both an explicit and a fixed cost.
Implicit cost is the cost of self-supplied factors, such as a farmer using their own tractor. No money is paid, but its value is worked out at market rates.
AC = TC ÷ output; it is the cost per unit. Example: TFC ₹180 and TVC ₹300 for 48 units gives TC ₹480 and AC = 480 ÷ 48 = ₹10.

MC is the increase in TC when output rises by one unit. It is calculated between two successive levels of output. Example: 10 shirts cost ₹1,110 and 11 shirts cost ₹1,199, so MC = ₹89, with AC ₹111 and ₹109.

Revenue is the money a seller receives by selling a quantity of a commodity: TR = Price × Quantity. TR is also called total sales proceeds. For several goods, add the TR of each. Example: 100 kg rice at ₹35 + 70 L oil at ₹90 + 150 kg flour at ₹22 + 100 packets of biscuits at ₹10 = ₹3,500 + ₹6,300 + ₹3,300 + ₹1,000 = ₹14,100.
AR = TR ÷ Q = P, so average revenue is the same as price.

MR is the increase in TR from selling one more unit: MR = TR(n) − TR(n−1). If every unit sells at the same price, AR = MR. Example: 10 kg at ₹30 gives TR ₹300 and 11 kg at ₹29 gives TR ₹319, so MR = ₹19.
Profit is the surplus of revenue over cost: Profit = TR − TC. Example: 50 units at ₹10 gives TR ₹500; TC = 110 + 150 = ₹260; so profit = ₹240.

or: What is meant by cost of production?
Cost of production is the money expenditure a producer incurs to buy or hire factors of production (land, labour, capital) and raw materials to produce goods and services.

sa: Distinguish between explicit cost and implicit cost.

Explicit cost: money actually paid out for fixed and variable factors and raw materials — rent, wages and raw materials. These are direct payments, recorded with bills and receipts.
Implicit cost: the cost of the producer's own self-supplied factors, e.g. a farmer's own tractor or land. No money is paid; its value is estimated at market rates (the ₹3,000 rent the tractor could have earned).
Distinguish between fixed cost and variable cost with examples.

Fixed cost is spending on fixed factors. It does not change with output and must be paid even at zero output, e.g. rent of land or a tractor.
Variable cost is spending on variable factors. It changes with output, e.g. wages and raw materials. A farmer paid ₹18,000 in wages when 4 workers were needed and ₹9,000 when only 2 were needed.
A firm produces 50 units sold at ₹10 each. Its fixed cost is ₹110 and variable cost ₹150. Find the profit.
A shopkeeper sells 10 kg of rice at ₹30 a kg, or 11 kg at ₹29 a kg. Find AR in each case and MR.

TR at 10 kg = 10 × 30 = ₹300, so AR = ₹30.
TR at 11 kg = 11 × 29 = ₹319, so AR = ₹29.
MR = 319 − 300 = ₹19.
AR equals the price; MR differs from AR because the price fell.
la: What is meant by cost? Distinguish between explicit cost and implicit cost.

Cost is the money a producer spends to buy or hire factors of production and raw materials. It is the producer's sacrifice.
Explicit cost: actual money payments to outsiders for land, labour, capital and raw materials — rent, wages, interest and material bills. They are direct, properly calculated and recorded.
Implicit cost: the value of factors the producer owns and uses, e.g. their own land, tractor or labour. Nothing is paid, but it is estimated at the market price the factor could have earned. Both must be counted to know the true cost.
Explain TR, AR and MR with a numerical example. Why are AR and price the same?

TR = P × Q, the total money received from sales.
AR = TR ÷ Q, the revenue per unit.
MR = TR(n) − TR(n−1), the extra revenue from one more unit.
Example: guavas at ₹50 a kg. 20 kg gives TR = ₹1,000 and AR = ₹50. 21 kg gives TR = ₹1,050 and MR = ₹50.
AR = (P × Q) ÷ Q = P, so average revenue always equals price. When every unit sells at the same price, MR = AR.
Explain TC, AC and MC with an example.

TC = TFC + TVC.
AC = TC ÷ output, the cost per unit.
MC = the increase in TC from one more unit of output.
Example: a tailor's TC is ₹1,110 for 10 shirts and ₹1,199 for 11 shirts.
AC = 1,110 ÷ 10 = ₹111 and 1,199 ÷ 11 = ₹109.
MC = 1,199 − 1,110 = ₹89.
AC is worked out at each level of output; MC is worked out between two successive levels.
